next.name: Break the Algorithm
next.tagline: Every algorithm has an input that defeats it.

cards.objective: Show a concrete input before any algorithm
cards.statement: An array of numbers. One simple job. Watch how the algorithm decides.

cards.objective: Prime the learner to think about the scanning strategy

interaction.prompt: How would an algorithm find the maximum?

options.label: Sort everything first
options.explanation: Sorting does more work than the job needs — it computes far more than the answer.

options.label: Compare while scanning, keep the biggest
options.explanation: One pass. Remember the best seen so far, compare as you go.

options.label: Check every pair
options.explanation: Comparing every pair is far more work than a single pass requires.

cards.reveal: A single scan, remembering the best so far, is all it takes.

cards.objective: Show the algorithm executing step by step
cards.statement: Watch the pointer scan. max only changes when a bigger value appears. Follow i, max and comparisons.

cards.objective: Check that the learner can count comparisons

interaction.prompt: How many comparisons for five numbers?

options.explanation: max starts at a[0], so each of the remaining 4 elements gets compared.
The first element sets the initial max — it is not compared with itself.
Every element after the first gets one comparison: that is 4, not 3.

cards.reveal: 5 numbers → 4 comparisons. Work tracks the input size.

cards.objective: Show comparisons growing with input size
cards.statement: Double the array and the work roughly doubles. The relationship is one-to-one.

cards.objective: Highlight the operation that dominates the cost
cards.statement: Everything else is bookkeeping. The comparison is the operation that happens most — it dominates.

cards.objective: Introduce O(n) as the name for this behavior
cards.statement: About n operations. That behavior has a name.
cards.footnote: Linear time — work grows in proportion to the input.

cards.objective: Show the best case for linear search
cards.statement: The target sits at the very front. One comparison and it is done.

cards.objective: Show the worst case for linear search
cards.statement: The target hides at the very end. The whole array gets scanned first.

cards.objective: Show typical behavior when the target sits somewhere in the middle
cards.statement: On a typical input the target sits somewhere in between — about half the array gets scanned.

cards.objective: Let the learner run the algorithm on their own input
cards.hook: Your turn to choose the input.
cards.statement: Type any array — watch the same algorithm execute against your data.

interaction.prompt: Type an array of numbers, separated by commas.
